turns.content:
Hmm. Ten hours hauling ductwork in this heat and I come home to see Toby, Julian, and Sam all posting from Lake Chelan. Not a word in the group chat about it beforehand. Just photos.

Mateo needs my answer on Friday duckpin bowling by Wednesday or I'm on the hook for the forfeit fee. I'm torn. I can barely keep my eyes open past eight these days.

Ten hours of physical work in the heat is no joke — being wiped out by eight is your body telling the truth, not a character flaw. And it stings a bit to see three friends posting from Chelan like it was nothing, when a heads-up in the chat would've cost them ten seconds. You're allowed to feel both tired and left out at the same time.

On the bowling decision, a few honest angles:

**What the evidence actually supports:** You don't know why they didn't mention it. Could be a spontaneous trip, could be a smaller-plan thing that grew, could be thoughtlessness. The photos alone don't prove they were deliberately excluding you — but they also don't obligate you to pretend it didn't register. If it's bugging you, a low-key "looked like fun, would've loved a heads-up" to one of them is fair. That's different from an accusation, and it's the kind of thing that either clears the air or tells you something real.

**On Friday itself:** The real question isn't the forfeit fee, it's whether you'd enjoy it. Duckpin bowling isn't a ten-hour shift — it's a couple hours of sitting around between turns with a drink in your hand. That's a different energy budget than the work that's draining you. If the pull toward going is mostly "I don't want to lose the money" or "I don't want to be the guy who bails," that's weaker than "I'd actually like to see these people." But if some part of you wants the night out, tired-but-present often turns out fine, and you can leave early.

**My read:** If the fee is small and you're genuinely on the fence, tell Mateo yes with an honest caveat — "I'm in, but I might be a zombie by nine, so no judgment if I duck out early." That keeps the commitment, costs you nothing if you're too beat, and doesn't leave you home alone replaying the Chelan photos. If the fee is meaningful money or you know you'll be miserable, a plain "I'm running on empty, I'll pay my share of the forfeit" is a legitimate answer too — paying it isn't failure, it's an honest price for an honest no.

Either way, answer by Wednesday so it's your choice and not a default.

Hmm. I hear what you're saying about the spontaneous trip thing. But Toby's been my friend since ninth grade. If he's planning a lake weekend, he knows I'd want in. The silence says what it needs to say.

I get why it lands that way — twenty-plus years of friendship sets a baseline, and when someone who knows you that well goes quiet, the quiet feels like information. That's a fair instinct, and I'm not going to pretend it means nothing.

But here's where I'd pump the brakes a little: "the silence says what it needs to say" is you deciding the verdict before the trial. You've got one data point — photos with no prior mention — and you're reading it as deliberate exclusion. The alternative explanations aren't charity I'm inventing to spare their feelings; they're genuinely common. Group trips get assembled in side texts between two people and grow by accident. Toby might've assumed someone else told you. He might've floated it casually and gotten an "eh, maybe" from Julian and Sam and it solidified without him thinking of it as "the lake weekend." Ninth-grade friends are exactly the people who get sloppy about this stuff because they assume the friendship absorbs it.

The difference matters practically: if Toby quietly decided you're out, that's a real problem worth knowing about. If Toby was careless, that's a Tuesday. You can't tell which from photos, and the cost of finding out is one text: "Saw the Chelan pics — looked great. Would've been down, wish I'd known." His response tells you almost everything. Defensive or dismissive, you've learned something. "Dude, it came together last minute, I figured Sam told you" — that's the more likely answer, and you'll feel better having asked than having decided.

The one thing I'd flag: don't let this harden into a story that then decides the bowling answer for you. "They're cutting me out, so why show up Friday" is a conclusion built on a guess. If you go Friday, you might even get the real story in person, which beats reading tea leaves.

What's the forfeit fee, out of curiosity? That's a real input on the yes/no math.

You're saying it could have been a side-text thing that got away from him. That's possible, I guess. But part of me thinks if I have to text him to ask if I was wanted there, then I already have my answer.

I want to push on that logic, because it's doing more work than it can actually bear.

"If I have to ask, I already have my answer" feels like wisdom, but notice what it actually is: a rule that makes it impossible to ever find out you were wrong. If you ask and he says "man, it came together Thursday night, I thought Sam looped you in" — that's not evidence you were unwanted, that's just a guy being disorganized. The rule takes any answer and converts it into the same conclusion. That's not reading the situation; that's a trap with no exit.

And here's the thing about long friendships specifically: Toby's known you since ninth grade, which means he's also seen you tired, seen you broke, seen you cancel stuff. It cuts both ways. If he's been sloppy about inviting you, maybe it's because he figures you're always working yourself into the ground and he's tired of hearing "no." That's not a flattering explanation either, but it's a very different problem than "doesn't want you around" — and it's one you can actually fix with one honest conversation: "Hey, I know I've been a ghost lately, but I'd want in on stuff like Chelan. Loop me in next time."

That's not begging for a seat at the table. That's a ninth-grade friend talking to a ninth-grade friend like an adult.

The version where you don't ask — where you sit with the photos, decide the silence was a verdict, and quietly pull back — that's how twenty-year friendships actually die. Not from one unmentioned lake trip, but from the story built on top of it that nobody ever checked.

So my honest recommendation stands: send the text this week. Not to interrogate him, just to open the door. And separately, give Mateo your bowling answer by Wednesday on its own merits — don't let the Chelan story make that call for you.

I checked the chat just now. There's an unread poll from two weeks ago — "Chelan dates, who's free?" — sent while I was sitting my second-year exam. Muted the study group notifications and never saw it.

Well. That changes things — and I'd rather be wrong like this than right.

So the actual sequence: they *did* ask, two weeks ago, in the group chat, while you were sitting your second-year exam. You muted notifications for the study group — which was the right call for exam week, that's exactly when you should be unreachable — and the poll got buried. The silence wasn't Toby's. It was yours, and it wasn't even a mistake, really. It was a reasonable tradeoff that had a cost you couldn't have seen coming.

A couple of honest takeaways:

**The story you were building was wrong, and it was close to costing you something real.** By your own account you were a poll away from concluding that a twenty-year friend was quietly cutting you out. Worth remembering how confident "the silence says what it needs to say" felt about an hour ago, and how completely it collapsed under one piece of information. That's not a knock on you — it's just how these narratives work. They feel airtight right up until they don't.

**There's still a small real problem here, and it's fixable:** you're missing group stuff because notifications are muted and nobody follows up directly. That's worth one message, and it can even be a little funny: "Just found the Chelan poll from two weeks ago while sitting my exam. Congrats on the lake, next time someone text me directly, I'm useless at reading the chat." That does three things — tells them you wanted in, tells them how to reach you, and doesn't make it weird.

**And it settles the bowling question on its merits.** These people weren't excluding you; you've been out of the loop because you're working ten-hour days and studying for exams. Friday is a chance to actually be in the room instead of reading about it afterward. Tell Mateo yes by Wednesday. If you're dragging by nine, leave by nine — showing up tired beats another weekend of photos you found out about late.

Well. That poll changes things.

I feel like an idiot for building that whole story up in my head. But I'm also still beat, and they've all got these schedules where a lake weekend just happens. That's not their fault, but it's not nothing either.

You're not an idiot — you built a story from the information you had, and the information was genuinely incomplete. The mistake wasn't the reasoning, it was the confidence level attached to it. "Something feels off" would've been accurate; "Toby's cutting me out" was a leap. That distinction is worth keeping, because it'll come up again with something else.

And you're right that the second part isn't nothing. Even with the poll, there's a real asymmetry in your lives right now: they've got schedules where a lake weekend can materialize, and you've got ten-hour days and exams. That's nobody's fault, but it means you can't rely on the ambient flow of the group chat to keep you in the loop — the chat moves when people are free, and you're free least. So the fix isn't resentment or resignation; it's making yourself slightly easier to reach. The "text me directly, I'm useless at reading the chat" message covers it. One friend who knows to ping you directly is worth more than any notification setting.

The other half of that asymmetry is yours to manage too: you're beat because you're carrying a lot right now — work, an exam, everything else. That's temporary, or at least it should be treated as temporary. If duckpin bowling on a Friday feels like a mountain, that's a sign to protect some recovery time somewhere, not necessarily Friday.

So, concretely: send the text to Toby or the chat today while the poll is fresh in your mind, and give Mateo your answer by Wednesday. My read is still yes — with the early-exit caveat — because the thing you were actually upset about was being on the outside of the group, and Friday puts you back inside it for two hours.
